title: Value types in C#
body: Which of the following is a **value type** in C#?

options.e: string is a reference type (with value-like equality).
Arrays are always reference types, even arrays of value types.
DateTime is a struct, so it is a value type.
object is the root reference type.

answer: DateTime — it is a struct.
explanation: Value types (structs, enums and the built-in numeric types) hold their data directly and are copied on assignment. Reference types (classes, arrays, delegates, string, object) hold a reference to an object on the managed heap. `DateTime`, `Guid`, `TimeSpan` and `decimal` are common BCL structs.

title: String immutability
body: What does this code print?
answer: hello
explanation: Strings are immutable. `b += " world"` creates a **new** string and assigns it to `b`; `a` still refers to the original "hello" instance. This is why repeated concatenation in loops should use `StringBuilder`.

title: const vs readonly
body: Which statement correctly describes `const` and `readonly` fields?

options.t: Both are evaluated at runtime and can be set in any method
const values are compile-time constants copied into calling assemblies; readonly fields are assigned at runtime in their declaration or a constructor
readonly fields are implicitly static and const fields are per-instance
const can hold any reference type initialised with new

answer: const = compile-time constant (implicitly static, baked into callers); readonly = set once at runtime (declaration or constructor).
explanation: `const` must be a compile-time constant of a primitive, enum or string type and is implicitly static. Because its value is embedded into the IL of consuming assemblies, changing a public const requires recompiling consumers. `readonly` fields can be instance or static, can hold any type, and are assigned in the declaration or a constructor — useful for values known only at runtime such as configuration or injected dependencies.

title: Parameterless struct constructors
body: True or false: since C# 10 a `struct` may declare an explicit parameterless constructor.

options.e: C# 10 added explicit parameterless constructors and field initializers for structs.

answer: True.
explanation: Before C# 10 structs always had an implicit parameterless constructor that zero-initialised all fields. C# 10 allows declaring one explicitly. Note that `default(MyStruct)` and array elements still bypass it and are zero-initialised.

title: Comparing strings with ==
body: What does `==` compare when both operands are of type `string`?

options.t: The memory addresses of the two strings
Their character content, because string overloads the == operator

answer: Their content — `string` overloads `==` to perform an ordinal value comparison.
explanation: For most reference types `==` compares references, but `System.String` overloads `==` and `!=` to compare values (ordinal, case-sensitive). If one operand is typed as `object`, the overload is not used and the comparison becomes a reference comparison — a classic bug. Use `string.Equals(a, b, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)` for case-insensitive checks.

title: Interfaces vs abstract classes
body: Which statement is true in modern C# (8.0 and later)?

options.t: A class can inherit from several abstract classes
options.e: C# supports single class inheritance only.

options.t: Interfaces can provide default method implementations but cannot declare instance fields

options.e: They can; constructors run when a derived class is instantiated.

options.t: Interface members are private by default
options.e: Interface members are public by default.

answer: Interfaces may have default implementations (C# 8+) but no instance state; a class inherits from one base class.
explanation: Use an abstract class when related types share state and implementation; use interfaces to describe capabilities that unrelated types can implement (a class can implement many). Default interface methods help evolve interfaces without breaking implementers, but interfaces still cannot hold instance fields.

title: override vs new
body: What does this program print?
answer: BA
explanation: `B.Name` **overrides** the virtual method, so a call through an `A` reference dispatches to `B` at runtime. `C.Name` uses `new`, which **hides** the base method: the call is bound at compile time to the static type `A`, so `A.Name` runs. Hiding with `new` rarely expresses the intent and usually indicates a design smell.

title: Dictionary lookup complexity
body: What is the average time complexity of `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>.TryGetValue`?
answer: O(1) on average.
explanation: `Dictionary` is a hash table: the key's `GetHashCode` selects a bucket and `Equals` resolves collisions. With a good hash distribution lookups are O(1) on average; many colliding keys degrade it towards O(n). `SortedDictionary` (a red-black tree) gives O(log n) with ordered keys.

title: Collections that enforce uniqueness
body: Which collections **reject duplicate elements**? Select all that apply.

options.e: Also a set, kept in sorted order.

answer: HashSet<T> and SortedSet<T>.
explanation: Set types model mathematical sets: `Add` returns `false` instead of inserting a duplicate. `HashSet<T>` offers O(1) average membership tests; `SortedSet<T>` keeps elements ordered with O(log n) operations. Dictionary keys are also unique.

title: Generic variance
body: Why does `IEnumerable<object> items = new List<string>();` compile, while `List<object> items = new List<string>();` does not?

options.t: List<T> is a class and classes can never be converted
IEnumerable<T> is declared covariant (out T); List<T> is invariant because it also accepts T as input
The first line compiles only with an explicit cast

answer: IEnumerable<out T> is covariant; List<T> is invariant.
explanation: Covariance (`out T`) is safe when T only flows **out** of the type — you can read strings as objects. `List<T>` also lets you **write** T (`Add`), so treating a `List<string>` as `List<object>` would allow adding an `int`. Variance is supported only on interfaces and delegates, and only for reference type arguments.

title: Deferred execution
body: What does this code print?

options.e: The query runs at Count(), after 4 was added: 2, 3, 4.

explanation: Most LINQ operators (`Where`, `Select`, …) use **deferred execution**: they build a query that runs when enumerated. `Count()` enumerates after `4` was added, so the result is 3 (values 2, 3, 4). Call `ToList()` to snapshot results, and beware of enumerating an expensive query multiple times.

title: Single() semantics
body: What happens when `Single()` is called on a sequence that contains more than one element?
answer: It throws InvalidOperationException.
explanation: `Single()` asserts the sequence has **exactly one** element and throws if it is empty or has more. `SingleOrDefault()` returns default for an empty sequence but still throws for more than one. `First()` / `FirstOrDefault()` just take the first match. Use `Single` when duplicates would indicate a data bug you want to surface.

title: IQueryable vs IEnumerable
body: What is the key difference between `IQueryable<T>` and `IEnumerable<T>`?

options.t: IQueryable builds an expression tree that a provider (e.g. EF Core) translates, such as into SQL; IEnumerable operators run as in-memory delegates
IEnumerable cannot be used with LINQ
IQueryable executes immediately while IEnumerable is deferred

answer: IQueryable carries expression trees for a query provider to translate; IEnumerable executes LINQ in memory.
explanation: With `IQueryable`, filters like `Where` become part of the SQL sent to the database. Calling `AsEnumerable()` or `ToList()` too early switches to LINQ-to-Objects, so subsequent filtering happens in memory after loading more rows than needed. Both are deferred.

title: What the event keyword adds
body: Compared with a public delegate field, what does declaring a member with the `event` keyword change?

options.t: Events can only have one subscriber
Outside code can only subscribe (+=) and unsubscribe (-=); only the declaring type can raise or reassign it

answer: It encapsulates the delegate: external code may only += / -=.
explanation: With a public delegate field, any caller could overwrite all subscribers with `=` or invoke the delegate. `event` restricts external access to add/remove accessors, enforcing the publisher/subscriber contract. Remember to unsubscribe from long-lived publishers to avoid memory leaks.

title: Func delegate signature
body: What does `Func<int, int, string>` represent?

options.t: A method taking a string and returning two ints
A method taking two int parameters and returning a string
A method taking three parameters and returning void

answer: Two int inputs, string return value — the last type argument of Func is the return type.
explanation: `Func<..., TResult>` delegates return a value (last type parameter); `Action<...>` delegates return void; `Predicate<T>` returns bool. Lambdas like `(a, b) => (a + b).ToString()` convert to these delegate types.

title: What await does
body: When execution reaches `await` on a task that has **not** completed, what happens?

options.t: The current thread blocks until the task completes
The method returns to its caller and the remainder runs as a continuation when the task completes
A new thread is always created to run the rest of the method

answer: Control returns to the caller; the rest of the method is scheduled as a continuation.
explanation: `await` does not block. The compiler turns the method into a state machine; if the awaitable is incomplete, the method returns an incomplete Task and resumes later (on the captured SynchronizationContext if any, otherwise the thread pool). This frees the thread to serve other work — the main benefit for I/O-bound server code.

title: Sync-over-async deadlock
body: Why can calling `.Result` on an incomplete task deadlock in a UI app or classic ASP.NET (with a synchronization context)?

options.t: The blocked thread owns the synchronization context that the awaited continuation needs to resume on, so neither can proceed
Because the task is garbage collected
Because .Result always starts the task twice

answer: The continuation waits for the context the blocked thread is holding.
explanation: The async method captured a single-threaded SynchronizationContext. `.Result` blocks that thread; when the awaited operation completes, the continuation is posted to the same context and never runs. ASP.NET Core has no SynchronizationContext, but blocking still wastes thread-pool threads and can cause starvation. Prefer async all the way; `ConfigureAwait(false)` in libraries.

title: Running independent calls concurrently
body: Which approach runs three independent I/O-bound calls concurrently?

options.t: await each call one after another
Start all three tasks, then await Task.WhenAll(t1, t2, t3)
Call .Wait() on each task in a loop

answer: Start the tasks first, then `await Task.WhenAll(...)`.
explanation: Awaiting sequentially makes total latency the sum of all calls. Creating the tasks first lets the I/O overlap, so latency becomes roughly the slowest call. `Task.Run` is for CPU-bound work and adds nothing for I/O. Handle failures: `await Task.WhenAll` throws the first exception; inspect each task for details, and pass a CancellationToken.

title: When async void is acceptable
body: When is an `async void` method appropriate?

options.t: For any method that does not return a value
Only for event handlers, because callers cannot await it or catch its exceptions

answer: Event handlers only.
explanation: An `async void` method cannot be awaited, so the caller cannot know when it completes, and exceptions are raised on the SynchronizationContext (often crashing the process). Use `async Task` everywhere else.

title: await inside lock
body: Why does the compiler reject `await` inside a `lock` block?

options.t: Monitor-based locks are thread-affine; after await the continuation may run on another thread that does not own the lock
Because await always throws inside try blocks
It is allowed; the compiler accepts it

answer: Monitor locks must be released by the acquiring thread; await may resume elsewhere (error CS1996).
explanation: Holding a lock across an await could also block other threads for unbounded time. For async mutual exclusion use `SemaphoreSlim(1, 1)` with `await WaitAsync()` and release in `finally`.

title: Large Object Heap
body: Which objects are allocated on the Large Object Heap (LOH) in .NET?
answer: Objects of at least 85,000 bytes.
explanation: The LOH holds large objects (≥ 85,000 bytes, typically big arrays/strings). It is collected with generation 2 and is not compacted by default, so frequent large allocations cause fragmentation and expensive gen-2 GCs. Pool buffers with `ArrayPool<T>` to reduce LOH pressure.

title: using declarations
body: What does a `using` statement or declaration guarantee for an `IDisposable`?

options.t: The object is garbage collected immediately
Dispose is called when the scope exits, even if an exception is thrown
The object can no longer be referenced
The object's finalizer is suppressed automatically

answer: Dispose runs at scope exit (compiled to try/finally).
explanation: `using` compiles to a try/finally that calls `Dispose()`. It releases unmanaged resources (file handles, sockets, DB connections) deterministically; it does not free managed memory. Use `await using` for `IAsyncDisposable`.

title: GC and Dispose
body: True or false: the garbage collector automatically calls `Dispose()` on unreachable objects that implement `IDisposable`.

options.e: The GC only runs finalizers; Dispose must be called explicitly.

answer: False.
explanation: The GC knows nothing about `IDisposable`. It may run a **finalizer** (`~ClassName`) on objects that declare one, at an unpredictable time. The dispose pattern calls `GC.SuppressFinalize(this)` in `Dispose` so the finalizer is skipped when cleanup already happened.

title: throw vs throw ex
body: In a catch block, what is the difference between `throw;` and `throw ex;`?

options.t: `throw;` rethrows preserving the original stack trace; `throw ex;` resets the stack trace to the current location

answer: `throw;` preserves the original stack trace.
explanation: Use `throw;` to rethrow. `throw ex;` loses where the exception originated, making diagnostics hard. To wrap, throw a new exception with the original as `InnerException`. `ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture(ex).Throw()` preserves the trace across threads.

title: finally blocks
body: Which statement about a `finally` block is correct?

options.t: It runs only when no exception occurs
It runs whether or not an exception is thrown, including when try contains a return statement
It runs before the catch block
It can change the value already returned by return in try for value types

answer: It always runs when control leaves the try (normal exit, return or exception).
explanation: finally is for cleanup. Exceptions: it may not run if the process terminates (e.g. `Environment.FailFast`, stack overflow).

title: Extension method requirements
body: What is required to declare an extension method?

options.t: A static method in a non-generic static class whose first parameter is prefixed with `this`
A method in a partial class

answer: Static method, static (non-nested, non-generic) class, `this` modifier on the first parameter.
explanation: Extension methods are syntactic sugar for static calls; they only see public members and are resolved at compile time when their namespace is imported. Instance methods always win over extensions with the same signature.

title: Cost of reflection
body: What is the main performance cost of reflection-based member access?

options.t: Runtime metadata lookup and late-bound invocation are much slower than compiled calls

answer: Metadata lookups and late-bound invocation are slow compared with direct calls.
explanation: Cache `MethodInfo`/`PropertyInfo`, or compile delegates/expression trees once and reuse them. Source generators eliminate runtime reflection entirely and are trim/AOT-friendly (e.g. System.Text.Json source generation).

title: Boxing and unboxing
body: Explain **boxing** and **unboxing** in C#. When do they happen, what do they cost, and how can you avoid them?
answer: Boxing wraps a value type in a heap object (e.g. assigning int to object); unboxing copies it back with an explicit cast.
explanation:
**Boxing** allocates an object on the heap and copies the value into it when a value type is converted to `object` or an interface it implements (e.g. `object o = 42;`, passing a struct to a non-generic `ArrayList`, calling `string.Format("{0}", 42)` in older APIs). **Unboxing** is the explicit cast back (`int i = (int)o;`) which checks the type and copies the value.

Costs: a heap allocation, a copy and extra GC pressure — significant in hot loops.

Avoid it with generics (`List<int>` instead of `ArrayList`), generic constraints, overloads that take the value type, and by implementing `IEquatable<T>` on structs so `Equals(T)` does not box.
reference: Boxing converts a value type instance to object or to an interface type it implements by allocating a heap object and copying the value. Unboxing is the explicit conversion back, which verifies the runtime type and copies the value out. Boxing costs an allocation and GC work; it happens implicitly with non-generic collections, object parameters and interface calls on structs. Generics, typed overloads and IEquatable<T> avoid it.

title: Reducing latency of chained service calls
body: An ASP.NET Core endpoint calls three independent downstream services **sequentially**; each takes ~300 ms. Describe how you would reduce the endpoint's latency and what failure cases you would handle.
answer: Run the calls concurrently with Task.WhenAll, propagate CancellationToken, add timeouts/retries via resilience policies, and decide how partial failures are handled.
explanation:
1. Start all three calls without awaiting, then `await Task.WhenAll(...)`: latency drops from ~900 ms to ~300 ms.
2. Use typed `HttpClient`s from `IHttpClientFactory` with timeouts, retries with jitter and a circuit breaker (Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience / Polly).
3. Pass the request's `CancellationToken` so abandoned requests stop work.
4. Decide on partial failure: fail fast, or return degraded data for optional calls (catch per task).
5. Consider caching results that change rarely, and measure with distributed tracing before and after.
reference: Execute independent I/O concurrently (Task.WhenAll), use IHttpClientFactory with timeout, retry with backoff and circuit breaker, flow CancellationToken, handle partial failures explicitly (fallbacks for optional data), cache stable data, and verify with tracing/metrics.

title: Modifying a list while iterating
body: What happens when this code runs, and how would you fix it?

options.t: It throws InvalidOperationException: Collection was modified
options.e: List<T> enumerators detect modification and throw.

answer: InvalidOperationException; use `list.RemoveAll(n => n % 2 == 0)` or iterate backwards with a for loop.
explanation: `List<T>` tracks a version number; modifying the list invalidates active enumerators and the next `MoveNext` throws. Fixes: `list.RemoveAll(predicate)`, a reverse `for` loop, or build a new list with LINQ (`list.Where(n => n % 2 != 0).ToList()`).
